title: Chapter 39 — The Seven Closing Techniques for the Retail Floor
intro: Seven proven closing techniques and the floor moments each one fits. These are not scripts. They are tools. Knowing when to use each one matters more than memorizing the words.

sections.title: Why Seven Techniques — Not One
sections.content:
If closing were simple, every salesperson would close every sale. The reality is that different customers need different approaches. Some need a gentle nudge. Some need urgency. Some need reassurance. Some just need to be asked.

Step 9 of the 10 Steps of Selling is Closing. Everything before it — engagement, rapport, discovery, needs, wants, recommendation, presentation, objection handling — sets the stage. These seven techniques are how you actually ask for the business once that stage is set.

No single technique works every time. The best salespeople read the customer and choose the right tool for the moment.

sections.title: Technique 1 — The Direct Ask
sections.content:
The simplest and most underused technique. You just ask.

'Would you like to take this home today?'
'Are we ready to move forward?'
'Shall we get this set up for delivery?'

When to use it: When the customer has been saying yes throughout the presentation, when they seem ready but nobody has asked, when the conversation has naturally reached its conclusion.

Why it works: A long-standing principle in sales is that many deals are lost simply because nobody asked. The direct ask removes ambiguity. The customer knows exactly what you are asking and can give you a clear answer.

Most salespeople avoid this because it feels too blunt. But it is actually the most respectful approach — you are not playing games or using tricks. You are asking a straightforward question.

sections.title: Technique 2 — The Alternative Close
sections.content:
Give the customer two options — both of which result in a sale.

'Would you prefer delivery on Tuesday or Thursday?'
'Would you like the stainless steel or the white?'
'Should we set this up with financing or would you prefer to pay in full today?'

When to use it: When the customer has decided to buy but has not committed to the details. When you want to move the conversation from if to when.

Why it works: It assumes the sale is happening and moves the conversation to logistics. The customer stops debating whether to buy and starts choosing how to buy. That is a much easier decision.

sections.title: Technique 3 — The Summary Close
sections.content:
Summarize everything they are getting and the value it represents, then ask for the commitment.

'So you are getting the 36-inch counter-depth French door refrigerator in stainless, with the flexible shelving and ice maker you wanted. We are including free delivery and installation. The extended warranty gives you five years of full coverage. And with the current promotion you are saving $400. Does everything look good to move forward?'

When to use it: When the customer seems overwhelmed by options. When there is a lot of value to highlight. When you want to remind them of everything they liked during the presentation.

Why it works: It packages the entire decision into one clear picture. Instead of a pile of features, prices, and options, the customer sees a complete solution. That clarity reduces hesitation.

sections.title: Technique 4 — The Urgency Close
sections.content:
Highlight a legitimate time-sensitive factor.

'This promotion ends on Saturday. After that, the price goes back up $300.'
'We only have two of these in stock. Once they are gone, the next shipment is six weeks out.'
'If we place the order today, we can guarantee delivery by next Friday. If we wait, the next available window is three weeks.'

When to use it: When there is a real, verifiable reason to act now. When the customer is ready but keeps postponing.

Why it works: It gives the customer a reason to decide today rather than next week. But here is the critical rule — the urgency must be real. Never invent false scarcity. Never lie about stock levels or promotion deadlines. Customers who discover you lied will never trust you again. And they will tell other people.

Real urgency helps the customer. Fake urgency destroys your credibility.

sections.title: Technique 5 — The Little Yes Close
sections.content:
Build a series of small agreements that make the final yes feel natural.

'Do you like this refrigerator?' Yes.
'Does it meet everything you were looking for?' Yes.
'Can you see it in your kitchen?' Yes.
'Are you comfortable with the price?' Yes.
'Do you like the features?' Yes.
'Great — are we ready to do this today?'

When to use it: When the customer is cautious. When you need to build their confidence gradually. When you sense they want to buy but are not quite ready to commit all at once.

Why it works: Each small yes lowers the psychological barrier to the big yes. By the time you ask the final question, they have already agreed with every component of the decision. Saying yes one more time is easy.

sections.title: Technique 6 — The Concern Close
sections.content:
Address the customer's hesitation head-on, then ask.

'I can see you are thinking about it. Is there something specific that is holding you back?'

Then listen. Really listen. They might say price. They might say they need to check measurements. They might say their spouse needs to see it. Whatever it is, address it directly.

Once resolved: 'Now that we have that sorted out, are we ready to move forward?'

When to use it: When you sense resistance but the customer has not told you what the problem is. When they are stalling.

Why it works: It shows you care about their concerns — not just about making the sale. It also surfaces the real objection so you can solve it. Remember — customers often raise surface objections instead of the real concern. 'It is expensive' might actually mean 'I need my partner to agree.' This technique gets to the truth.

sections.title: Technique 7 — The Ownership Close
sections.content:
Help the customer mentally own the product before they buy it.

'Imagine it is Sunday morning. You walk into your kitchen and this refrigerator is sitting there. You pull out the French doors, grab your cold brew from the shelf you adjusted exactly where you want it. The kids are not even awake yet. That is your new morning.'

When to use it: When the customer is emotionally engaged. When wants matter more than needs. When you are selling a premium or luxury product.

Why it works: People buy emotionally and justify logically. Once the customer can picture the product in their life — not on the showroom floor — the decision becomes personal. They are no longer buying a refrigerator. They are buying a better version of their daily routine.

This technique is especially powerful for high-end sales where the product represents a lifestyle, not just a function.

sections.title: Matching the Technique to the Moment
sections.content:
The skill is not memorizing seven techniques. It is knowing which one fits right now.

Customer has been agreeing with everything? Direct Ask or Little Yes.
Customer is overwhelmed by options? Summary Close.
Customer is ready but stalling? Urgency Close — if the urgency is real.
Customer is cautious and holding back? Concern Close.
Customer is emotionally excited about the product? Ownership Close.
Customer has decided but has not picked the details? Alternative Close.

Sometimes you use one technique. Sometimes you use two or three in sequence. The conversation tells you which tools to reach for. That only works if you have been listening through all 10 Steps — because the close is built on everything that came before it.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating closing technique usage, ask:

Does the salesperson have more than one closing technique — or do they use the same approach every time?
Do they match the technique to the customer's state of mind?
Do they ask directly for the sale or rely on hints?
Do they use urgency honestly — or do they manufacture false deadlines?
Do they provide reassurance after the customer commits?
When a close fails, do they investigate what was missed in the earlier steps — or do they just blame the customer?

Closing is Step 9 of 10. It is not the most important step — it is the step that reveals whether the first eight were done well.
